USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep List 1 in force and let the already-finalized List 2 (25% on ~$16B, effective 23 August) proceed as announced, but do not lock in List 3 at 25% before the 20–23 August hearings and the 6 September comment deadline. Reopen a structured channel with Beijing now, using the pending $200B list as leverage rather than an automatic next shot. Insist on verifiable IP/tech-transfer remedies; do not trade another purchase-only communiqué for a pause, and do not unilaterally roll anything back.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modestly elevated, not high. The Section 301 record (22 March) still stands—China has not made structural IP concessions, and the 19 May joint statement (purchases only; Mnuchin “on hold”) collapsed on 29 May when Washington correctly refused to treat buy-more as a settlement. That unresolved practice is a real interest hit. Costs are also landing at home: China matched the 6 July $34B action with 25% duties aimed at soy, pork and other farm goods; nearly a third of U.S. soy (~$14B) goes to China, soybean prices fell more than 10% after the 15 June lists, and expected soybean profitability was reported down nearly $100/acre. Bilateral goods already show the squeeze—U.S. exports to China fell from $12.7B (March) to $9.3B (August, −27%) while imports from China were front-loaded from $38.3B to $47.8B, and the goods deficit widened to −$75.1B. CNY has depreciated from ~6.33 to 6.93 (+9.4% USD), blunting tariff incidence and further hurting U.S. exporters. That is why the score is above zero.

It is not a +0.5 reading. U.S. industrial production is still rising (104.0), VIX is ~14.6, and there is no recession signal. China is under more FX/reserve pressure (reserves −1%, yuan slide) and already used its best bilateral tariff room matching $50B; its 3 August $60B counter-list (5–25%) is contingent on List 3. ZTE’s April denial order showed non-tariff leverage, and the July settlement extracted a $1B fine, escrow, board change and monitors without giving away the 301 case. Immediate extra escalation (List 3 at 25% this week) would hit U.S. intermediates and consumer goods before hearings, invite the $60B Chinese list, and deepen farm-belt damage into harvest without a negotiating table. Immediate concession would repeat May. Hold-and-talk through the open List 3 process is the stance that matches a +0.2 threat: keep coercive inventory intact, convert it into a structural deal rather than a tariff cascade.
key_factors: Section 301 IP/tech-transfer findings remain unremedied after the May purchase-only truce collapsed

U.S. ag/soy is the main retaliatory pressure point; exports to China already down ~27%
U.S. macro still solid (IP up, low VIX); China absorbing more FX/reserve stress and yuan offset
List 3 ($200B, 10%→25%) is still in comment/hearings—best used as leverage, not fired this week
ZTE episode showed U.S. non-tariff leverage; do not spend it again without structural IP terms

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Implement the already-announced matching 25% on the remaining ~$16B when USTR List 2 takes effect on 23 August, and state clearly that a $200B List 3 — especially at 25% — will draw a prepared mix of remaining tariff space and qualitative measures. Do not launch unforced new tariff waves or a managed devaluation now, and do not revive the May purchase-commitment package unless Washington freezes List 3. Keep a negotiating channel open so a pause remains available if the U.S. wants one.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not existential. List 1 ($34B at 25%) is already in force with matching Chinese retaliation the same day (2018-07-06); USTR published List 3 (~$200B, ~6,000 lines) on 2018-07-10 and on 2018-08-01 said it is considering raising that rate from 10% to 25%; List 2 (~$16B at 25%) was finalized 7 August for 23 August. Section 301 is aimed at industrially significant / Made in China 2025 sectors, not consumer odds and ends. The April ZTE denial order showed U.S. component leverage over a major Chinese telecom, and the 13 August NDAA ban on U.S. government/contractor use of Huawei and ZTE continues firm-level tech pressure even after the commercial ZTE ban was lifted in July. FX is the clearest stress channel: DEXCHUS moved from ~6.34 in late February to 6.933 on 15 August (~9.4% weaker), the broad dollar is up ~7%, and Trump has already accused China of currency manipulation — so further engineered depreciation would invite a currency-war charge and capital-flight risk. That said, this is not +1.0: industrial production is still ~6% y/y (106.1), SA merchandise exports have not collapsed, and reserves remain ~$3.13tn with only about a 1% decline. Action should therefore be proportional retaliation, not maximal escalation or concession. China cannot match $200B+ in U.S. goods; the 19 May joint statement (China to “significantly increase” purchases; Mnuchin “on hold”) was discarded by the White House on 29 May; and analysts have judged a 2015-style devaluation too costly. Matching List 2 preserves credibility. Holding extra qualitative tools until List 3 is actually imposed avoids handing Washington a pretext for another $200B tranche, while talks can still be used to test a freeze.
